q: An SCR (thyristor) has:
explanation: SCR is a PNPN device with junctions J1, J2, J3 and terminals anode, cathode and gate.

q: The most common and reliable method of turning on an SCR is:
explanation: A positive gate pulse with the anode forward-biased is controlled and reliable. Breakover, dv/dt and thermal turn-on are undesirable/uncontrolled.

q: Once an SCR is conducting, the gate:
options: Loses control; the SCR stays on until current falls below holding current
Can turn it off with negative current
explanation: The SCR latches. It turns off only when anode current drops below the holding current (natural or forced commutation).
why: Anode current is set by the external circuit.
A pulse is enough once latching current is reached.

q: For an SCR, latching current is:
explanation: Latching current (minimum anode current to stay on just after turn-on, gate removed) is typically 2–3 times the holding current.

q: An RC snubber connected across an SCR protects it against:
explanation: The snubber limits the rate of rise of forward voltage that could falsely trigger the SCR via junction capacitance. A series inductor limits di/dt.

q: A TRIAC is equivalent to:
options: Two SCRs in anti-parallel with a common gate
A diode and an SCR in series
explanation: TRIAC conducts in both directions and is used for AC power control (fan regulators, light dimmers), often triggered by a DIAC.
why: Series SCRs do not conduct in reverse.

q: A DIAC is commonly used to:
explanation: A DIAC is a bidirectional breakover device that gives a sharp trigger pulse to the TRIAC gate.

q: A GTO thyristor differs from a conventional SCR because it:
options: Can be turned off by a negative gate current
explanation: Gate Turn-Off thyristors can be switched off by a large negative gate pulse, removing the need for forced commutation circuits.

q: An IGBT combines:
options: MOSFET input (voltage-controlled) and BJT-like output (low conduction loss)
explanation: IGBT has the high input impedance and easy gate drive of a MOSFET with the low on-state voltage of a bipolar device; used in inverters and motor drives.

q: Which power device has the highest switching frequency capability?
explanation: MOSFETs are majority-carrier devices with no stored charge, so they switch in tens to hundreds of nanoseconds — ideal for SMPS at high frequency.
why: GTOs are slow (a few hundred Hz to ~1 kHz).

q: A power MOSFET is a:
explanation: Gate-source voltage controls the channel; only majority carriers conduct, giving fast switching and a positive temperature coefficient of R_{DS(on)}.

q: A Schottky diode is preferred in low-voltage SMPS because it has:
options: Low forward voltage drop and negligible reverse recovery
explanation: Metal–semiconductor junction: ≈0.3 V forward drop and no minority-carrier storage, so it is fast and efficient at low voltages.
why: Schottky diodes have limited reverse ratings.

q: A fully controlled converter operates as a line-commutated inverter when the firing angle is:
explanation: For α > 90°, average DC voltage reverses (with current direction unchanged) and power flows from DC side to AC side — used in HVDC inverter stations and regenerative braking.

q: A free-wheeling diode across an inductive load of a controlled rectifier:
options: Prevents negative output voltage and improves input power factor
explanation: It provides a path for load current when the supply reverses, so the output is clamped at zero instead of going negative.
why: It removes the negative portions, raising the average.
It plays no part in triggering.

q: An inverter converts:
options: AC of one frequency directly to another
explanation: Inverters (VSI/CSI) produce AC from a DC source; used in UPS, motor drives, solar PV and HVDC.

q: Pulse-width modulation (PWM) in inverters is used to:
options: Control output voltage and reduce lower-order harmonics
explanation: Varying pulse widths controls the fundamental output and pushes harmonics to higher frequencies where they are easily filtered.
why: Switching losses are an unwanted side-effect.
DC link voltage is set by the rectifier/source.

q: A single-phase full-bridge square-wave inverter has V_{dc} = 220 V. RMS value of the fundamental output voltage is about:
why: That is the rms of the full square wave (all harmonics).
That is 220/√2 — sine rms with peak 220.

q: A cycloconverter converts:
options: AC at one frequency directly to AC at another (usually lower) frequency
explanation: No DC link: it synthesises a lower-frequency output from segments of the input; used for large low-speed drives (cement mills, ship propulsion).

q: An AC voltage controller (e.g. fan regulator using a TRIAC) changes:
options: RMS voltage at the same frequency
explanation: Phase-angle control chops part of each half-cycle, reducing rms voltage while the frequency stays at supply frequency.
why: That is a cycloconverter or inverter.
Not possible with a voltage controller.

q: In variable-frequency induction motor drives, V/f is kept constant to:
explanation: Air-gap flux ∝ V/f; constant flux avoids saturation at low frequency and maintains torque capability.
why: Speed changes with frequency — that is the aim.

q: A 400 V, 50 Hz induction motor is run by a constant V/f drive at 25 Hz. Supply voltage should be about:
why: Keeping 400 V would over-flux the motor.

q: A UPS of the online (double-conversion) type:
options: Feeds load directly from mains and switches to battery on failure
Continuously converts AC→DC→AC so the load is always fed by the inverter
explanation: Load is always on the inverter, giving zero transfer time and isolation from mains disturbances.
why: A UPS stores energy, usually in batteries.
Rotary UPS is a different technology.

q: Compared with a linear power supply, an SMPS:
options: Is smaller, lighter and more efficient because of high-frequency switching
explanation: Switching at tens–hundreds of kHz shrinks magnetics and capacitors; efficiency is typically 80–95%.

q: In a single-phase fully controlled converter with highly inductive load, the input (supply) power factor is approximately:
explanation: Input current is a square wave: displacement factor = cos α and distortion factor = 2√2/π ≈ 0.9, so pf ≈ 0.9 cos α.
why: That is only the displacement factor.

q: Which device is turned ON by a gate pulse but can be turned OFF only by reducing anode current (natural/forced commutation)?
explanation: SCR is a semi-controlled switch. MOSFET, IGBT and GTO are fully controlled (turn-on and turn-off by gate).
why: Turned off by negative gate current.

q: Forced commutation of SCRs is mainly needed in:
options: DC choppers and inverters fed from a DC source
explanation: On DC there is no natural current zero, so an auxiliary circuit must reverse-bias the SCR (or fully controlled devices are used).
why: AC supply reversal turns them off naturally.

q: With the anode positive with respect to the cathode, no gate signal and voltage below breakover, an SCR is in the:
explanation: With anode positive and no adequate gate trigger, J2 is reverse-biased and only leakage flows: forward blocking.
why: Reverse blocking needs the anode negative.
A normal SCR does not conduct in reverse.

q: An SCR is turned on by:
explanation: SCR gate is current-triggered; MOSFET/IGBT gates are voltage-controlled.

q: A UJT is commonly used in SCR circuits as a:
explanation: The UJT relaxation oscillator produces sharp pulses (via a pulse transformer) to fire SCRs.

q: In thyristor circuits, "commutation" means:
explanation: Commutation is the process of turning off a conducting thyristor — natural (line) or forced.

q: An RC snubber is connected:
options: In series with the load only
explanation: Across the device it limits dv/dt; series inductance limits di/dt.

q: The I^{2}t rating of a thyristor is used for:
explanation: The fuse’s total let-through I^{2}t must be less than the device’s I^{2}t rating to protect it during a fault.

q: A light-activated SCR is known as:
explanation: LASCR is triggered by light, giving electrical isolation (used in HVDC valves).
